title: Domestic inflation ‘a key risk’ for RBA
full_text:
Home-grown inflation is becoming the key risk for the Reserve Bank, with an appreciating Australian dollar boosting cheap imports – disguising dangerously high local cost pressures that businesses will look to pass on to consumers.
Ahead of the RBA board’s meeting this week to consider an interest change, moderating headline inflation figures have lowered market expectations for a 0.25-percentage-point hike by the end of this year to just 40 per cent.
The dollar has risen close to 9 per cent since the start of the year, making imports cheaper and helping to reduce headline inflation, with the central bank tipped to keep interest rates on hold.
However, economists are warning that care needs to be taken in focusing on headline inflation and greater consideration needs to be given to so-called non-tradeable inflation – where domestic cost pressures push up the price of goods and services in Australia.
Chief economist at currency risk manager Ebury Anthony Malouf said domestic inflation was a “key risk”.
“Non-tradeable inflation continues to be a persistent issue, with the annual rate sitting at 4.9 per cent year on year, or 5 per cent on a three-month annualised basis,” Mr Malouf said.
“This, in our view, remains a key risk to an otherwise improving inflation picture and will likely see the RBA remain relatively hawkish and not write off any chance of further rate hikes ahead,” Mr Malouf said.
Shadow Assistant Minister for Citizenship Dave Sharma says inflation has stayed above the RBA’s target band for the past three years, leaving Australia in an “unsustainable position”. “Inflation is still at 3.8 per cent; that is well out of the RBA’s target band of two to three per cent,” Mr Sharma told News24 host Sharri Markson. "It's also higher than any other, well, nearly all other advanced economies. “Australia is an outlier here, and it shows we are not on top of the inflation problem yet.” “The truth is, the RBA has pointed out that government spending, excessive government spending, keeps adding to inflationary pressures in Australia.”
Housing inflation also presents an upside risk, with the cost of building a new home rising 5.8 per cent in the past year – the highest rate of growth since mid-2023.
New home building costs account for the largest individual weight in the consumer price index.
IFM Investors chief economist Alex Joiner said labour costs were a key area for the RBA to gauge the domestic inflation problem.
“A tight labour market is exactly the channel through which domestically generated inflation persists – via wages, services pricing, second-round effects on inflation expectations,” Dr Joiner said.
“You don’t get comfortable declaring the [interest rate] cycle closed while that channel is still live,” he said.
Dr Joiner has set a target for the RBA to not only bring the closely monitored core inflation rate back to the central bank’s targeted 2.5 per cent, but for domestic inflation to also be firmly back within a range of 2 to 3 per cent.
“We think that the RBA’s job is not just to get trimmed mean CPI to print within the target band. It’s to push the domestically generated components of inflation durably back inside the 2–3 per cent band, such that once policy eases, they stay there,” he said.
HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham confirmed the bank’s base case forecast a slowdown in growth, further cooling in the housing market and a loosening labour market that would satisfy the RBA that no further rate hikes would be needed – though conceded there were risks to that assessment.
“We see the downswing in growth being sufficient that the RBA begins to cut its cash rate in H2 2027,” he said.
“However there is still some risk that core inflation does not fall fast enough and that the RBA chooses to hike again.”
